concept.body: Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C, where C sits BETWEEN sides a and b, and c faces C. Use for SAS (find the far side) or SSS (solve for cos C, then inverse-cos). Order matters: square both sides, sum, subtract the full 2ab·cos C product, then square-root. Negative cosine = obtuse angle, and C = 90° recovers Pythagoras.

explanationVariants: cos 90° = 0 removes the correction: c² = 36 + 64 = 100, c = 10.
With the included angle square, it IS Pythagoras: √(36 + 64) = 10.

widget.prompt: a = 6, b = 8, included angle C = 90°. Use the Law of Cosines to find c.

commonErrors.feedback: 14 = 6 + 8 adds plain lengths — the law adds SQUARES (then roots): √100 = 10.
100 is c². One more step — the square root: 10.

steps.body: Two sides hugging a known angle — SAS — leaves no matched pair for the Law of Sines. The Law of Cosines steps in: **c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C**, where C is the angle BETWEEN a and b, and c faces it. It's Pythagoras with a correction term that pays for the missing right angle.
The law of cosines is Pythagoras with a correction term.

widget.prompt: Sides 3 and 4. Open the angle until the third side is exactly 5.
widget.successFeedback: 90°, and the correction term −2ab·cos θ vanishes because cos 90° = 0 — leaving 3² + 4² = 5². Pythagoras is not a separate theorem; it is the law of cosines at the one angle where the correction disappears. Open the angle further and the third side grows beyond 5.
widget.lowFeedback: Under 5 — the angle is still acute, so the correction term is subtracting from a² + b².
widget.highFeedback: Over 5 — the angle is obtuse, so cosine has gone negative and the correction term is now ADDING.

predict.prompt: At what included angle does the law of cosines become the Pythagorean theorem?
predict.reveal: At 90°, cos 90° = 0, so the correction term disappears and a² + b² = c² remains. At 60° it survives: cos 60° = 0.5, so −2ab·cos C leaves −ab behind; at 0°, cos 0° = 1 keeps the full −2ab. Only where the cosine itself is zero does the law collapse to Pythagoras.

cml.actionGoal: Change the included angle and observe how the opposite side and cosine correction term covary.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Move past 90°. Why does the opposite side grow even though a and b do not change?

explanation.prompt: Why does the third side equal 5 exactly at 90°?

options.label: cos 90° is zero, so the correction term vanishes.
options.feedback: Exactly—the general law collapses to the Pythagorean theorem.

options.label: The third side is always the sum of the other two.
options.feedback: Triangle inequality prevents equality, and the relationship depends on the angle.

options.label: It is only a graphical rounding coincidence.
options.feedback: The equality is exact because the cosine term is exactly zero.

steps.body: Run SAS: a = 7, b = 9, C = 52°. Then c² = 49 + 81 − 2·7·9·cos 52° = 130 − 126·cos 52° ≈ 52.43, so c ≈ 7.24. Order of operations is the whole battle: square, sum, subtract the FULL product, and only then take the root.

widget.prompt: a = 7, b = 9, included angle C = 52°. Find side c (2 decimals).

commonErrors.feedback: 11.4 = √130 skips the correction term entirely — valid only at C = 90°. Subtract 126·cos 52° first: ≈ 7.24.
14.41 = √(130 + 126·cos 52°) flips the sign — the term SUBTRACTS for our formula's form. √52.43 ≈ 7.24.
52.43 is c², one step from done. Take the square root: ≈ 7.24.

steps.body: Given all three sides — SSS — solve the formula for the cosine instead: **cos C = (a² + b² − c²)/(2ab)**. A bonus signal rides along: a NEGATIVE cosine means C is obtuse. Sides 5, 7, 10: cos C = (25 + 49 − 100)/70 = −26/70 ≈ −0.3714 — obtuse before you even press inverse-cos.

explanationVariants: cos C = −26/70 ≈ −0.3714, so C = cos⁻¹(−0.3714) ≈ 111.8° — obtuse, as the negative promised.
The 10 faces the biggest angle: (25 + 49 − 100)/70 is negative, landing at ≈ 111.8°.

widget.prompt: Sides 5, 7, and 10. Find the angle OPPOSITE the 10, in degrees (1 decimal).

commonErrors.feedback: 68.2° = cos⁻¹(+0.3714) drops the minus sign — but 25 + 49 − 100 is NEGATIVE, and negative cosine means obtuse: ≈ 111.8°.
27.7° is the angle opposite the 5 — the sides got shuffled in the formula. The angle opposite the 10 puts 100 in the c² slot: ≈ 111.8°.

steps.body: Make the cosine sign change visible.

widget.prompt: Keep sides 5 and 12 fixed. Open the included angle until the third side is 13, then read the angle.
widget.successFeedback: The angle reaches 90°. Because 5² + 12² = 13², the law-of-cosines correction term vanishes exactly at a right angle.
widget.lowFeedback: The third side is under 13, so the included angle is still acute.
widget.highFeedback: The third side is over 13, so the included angle is obtuse.

explanationVariants: SAS has no side-angle matched pair, so the Law of Sines can't start — Cosines is built for exactly this.
Two sides + included angle → Cosines; a matched pair → Sines.

widget.prompt: You know two sides and the angle BETWEEN them. Which tool finds the third side?

options.label: Law of Cosines for a known SAS triangle
options.feedback: The included angle plugs straight into c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C.

options.label: Law of Sines for a known SAS triangle
options.feedback: Sines needs a side matched with its OPPOSITE angle — the included angle faces the side you don't have yet. Cosines first.

options.label: SOH-CAH-TOA for a known SAS triangle
options.feedback: The plain ratios require a right angle, which SAS doesn't promise. Cosines handles any included angle.

options.label: Pythagoras for a known SAS triangle
options.feedback: Only if the included angle is exactly 90° — otherwise you need the full formula with its correction term.

hints: The two legs (140 km and 90 km) hug the 118° turn angle between the paths — SAS.
d² = 140² + 90² − 2·140·90·cos 118° — note cos 118° is NEGATIVE, so the correction ADDS distance.
explanationVariants: d = √(27700 + 25200·0.4695) ≈ √39530.6 ≈ 198.82 km — more than √27700 ≈ 166, since the wide 118° pushes the endpoints apart.
With an obtuse included angle the correction term flips positive: d ≈ 198.82 km.

widget.prompt: A ship sails 140 km, turns so the two path segments meet at 118°, then sails 90 km. How far is it from the start (2 decimals)?

commonErrors.feedback: 166.43 = √(140² + 90²) ignores the angle — Pythagoras only rules at 90°. The 118° correction ADDS: ≈ 198.82.
125.97 ≈ √(27700 − 25200·0.4695) subtracts the magnitude — but cos 118° is already NEGATIVE, so the formula's − sign turns it into addition: ≈ 198.82.
230 = 140 + 90 measures the path SAILED, not the straight-line displacement asked: ≈ 198.82.

takeaways: SAS: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C, with C the INCLUDED angle.
SSS: cos C = (a² + b² − c²)/(2ab); a negative cosine flags an obtuse angle.
At C = 90° the correction dies and Pythagoras returns.
steps.teaser: Finale: choosing the right tool every time — plus a trig formula for area.
